paragraphs.heading: What it says
paragraphs.text: In elementary algebra, the binomial theorem tells you how to multiply out a power of a binomial such as x + y. Raising (x + y) to the power n gives a sum of terms that each look like axᵏʸᵐ. The exponents k and m are nonnegative whole numbers that add up to n. Each coefficient a is a positive whole number that depends on n and k, and these coefficients are called binomial coefficients.

paragraphs.heading: A worked case
paragraphs.text: For n = 4, the expansion is (x + y)⁴ = x⁴ + 4x³y + 6x²y² + 4xy³ + y⁴. Once like terms are gathered there are n + 1 terms. Their coefficients always add up to 2ⁿ.

paragraphs.heading: Seen as shapes
paragraphs.text: For positive a and b, the case n = 2 is something you can draw. Take a square whose side is a + b: it splits into two smaller squares, one with side a and one with side b, plus two rectangles that measure a by b. The case n = 3 does the same in three dimensions. A cube with side a + b breaks into two smaller cubes, with sides a and b, plus three boxes measuring a × a × b and three measuring a × b × b.

paragraphs.heading: Why the coefficients count choices
paragraphs.text: Multiplying out (x + y)ⁿ means taking either x or y from each of the n copies of the binomial. Only one term is xⁿ, the one where x is taken every time. But xⁿ⁻²y² turns up many times, once for each way of picking exactly two of the binomials to give a y. So after like terms are combined, its coefficient equals the number of ways to choose 2 elements from a set of n. Induction offers a second proof of the theorem.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond whole-number powers
paragraphs.text: The standard theorem deals only with exponents that are nonnegative whole numbers. A generalized version allows exponents that are not whole numbers, are negative, or are even complex, at the cost of turning the finite sum into an infinite series. When the exponent r is a nonnegative whole number, the coefficients for k > r are zero and the usual theorem comes back; for other r, infinitely many terms are nonzero. With r = −1, it gives 1/(1 + x) = 1 − x + x² − x³ + x⁴ − ⋯, the formula for a geometric series when |x| < 1.

paragraphs.heading: An old idea
paragraphs.text: Special cases were known by at least the 4th century BC, when Euclid mentioned the case n = 2. Around 510 AD, Aryabhata's method for finding cube roots suggests he knew the formula for n = 3. The Persian mathematician al-Karajī (953–1029) wrote a book, now lost, that held the theorem and a table of the coefficients. A clear statement appears in al-Samawʾal's 12th-century al-Bāhir, which credits it to al-Karajī. Yang Hui and Chu Shih-Chieh knew the expansions for small powers in the 13th century.

paragraphs.heading: Into modern mathematics
paragraphs.text: In 1544, Michael Stifel coined the term "binomial coefficient" and showed how to write (1 + x)ⁿ using (1 + x)ⁿ⁻¹, through Pascal's triangle. In the 17th century Blaise Pascal studied that triangle in depth in his Traité du triangle arithmétique. In 1664-5 Isaac Newton found the generalized theorem, which works for any real exponent, inspired by John Wallis's Arithmetic Infinitorum.
